elevated titers of four aPLA were found in 6. 9% of all AMI patients on hospitalization.
the presence of antiphospolipid antibodies is associated with acute myocardial infraction in the young population, especially in men.

the presence and role of antiphosphatidyl antibodies in young patients with acute myocardial infarcation.
the role of antiphosphatidyl antibodies in the pathogenesis of acute myocardial injury.
the role of antiphospho-lipid antibodies (anti-phospholipid autoimmunity) in acute myocardial ischemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a significant association between elevated titers of aCL, aPS, aPI and aPC in young patients' serum and the occurrence of AMI, and that aPLA may represent an additional risk factor in AMI.
there is an association of aPLA with AMI, but this is not a causal relationship.
there is no evidence of an increased prevalence of aPLA at hospital admission in patients with AMI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no correlation between the presence of elevated titers of aCL, aPS, aPI, aPC and aPEA with acute myocardial infraction in young patients.
the presence of elevated titers of aCL, aPS, aPI, aPC and aPEA at the early stages of AMI suggests the presence of an autoimmune phenomenon in this disease.

the presence of antiphospolipid antibodies at the onset of AMI in a young patient without apparent cardiovascular risk factor is an additional risk factor and the disappearance of these antibodies 3 months after MI suggests that the antibodies may have been present before the AM I.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of antiphospolipid antibodies is associated with a higher risk of myocardial infarctions, especially among younger patients without other risk factors.
the presence of antiphospolipid antibodies is a risk factor for acute myocardial infarcion, especially in the young.
the presence of aCL, aPS, aPI, aPC and aPEA antibodies in patients with AMI is associated with the younger age group and may be an additional independent risk factor for AM I.
